issues.title: Invalid universal standard-form representation
issues.failure_explanation: The old assertion says that every admissible vertically closed form has the displayed nearest-neighbour representation. But `eq:klform` permits independent differentials of arbitrary prolongation coordinates, whereas every term in `eq:multiform` contains one differential at shift \(-\mathbf1_i\) and one at shift zero. For example, with \(p=1,q=2\), the vertically closed form \(d_vu^1\wedge d_vu^2\) is conserved on solutions of the first-order system \(S u^\alpha=u^\alpha\), yet it cannot equal the displayed mixed-shift expression on the ambient prolongation space. Moreover, \(S_i^{-1}u^\alpha\) is not a coordinate on the stated space \(\mathbb Z^p\times U\).
issues.overall_effect: The claim that every multisymplectic form is automatically of the nearest-neighbour standard type fails. General multisymplectic forms may still be treated abstractly, and the standard formula remains valid when derived from the specified first-order quasilinear Lagrangian class.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Retract the assertion that every vertically closed conserved (p−1,2)-form has the nearest-neighbour expression in `eq:multiform`. State the general expansion on the prolongation space using arbitrary finite shift indices, as permitted by `eq:klform`, and reserve the displayed mixed-shift expression as the standard subclass arising from the specified first-order quasilinear Lagrangians, as established by `olol`. Remove the surrounding automatic-converse language.
issues.why_classification: The independence of vertical differentials at arbitrary shifts rules out any notational or local same-guarantee correction. Retaining universal scope requires abandoning the nearest-neighbour conclusion, while retaining that conclusion requires excluding a broad, natural class of multisymplectic forms. Thus every established repair loses the target's central universal normal-form guarantee, which is major mathematical loss even though the remaining abstract framework needs no global reconstruction.

issues.title: Multisymplectic-to-Lagrangian equivalence overclaim

failure_location.quote:
Now we are going to propose a systematic method, with which one can
proceed from a multisymplectic structure to an equivalent difference
Lagrangian structure.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: (However, these equations may be weaker than the given system and so admit other solutions.)

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims an equivalent Lagrangian structure, which implies equality of the original and Euler–Lagrange solution sets. The old argument actually establishes only that every original solution satisfies \(\mathcal E^\vartriangle(\mathscr L)=0\); it gives no reverse implication, and the paper's continuous analogue explicitly notes that the resulting equations may be weaker. Thus the supported relation is solution-set inclusion, not equivalence.
issues.overall_effect: The existence of a locally associated Lagrangian whose Euler–Lagrange equations contain all original solutions survives, but equivalence of the two systems does not. The later theorem for the explicitly Euler–Lagrange system in `el` does not require the missing converse.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace “equivalent difference Lagrangian structure” by a one-way associated-Lagrangian statement: the construction yields a local Lagrangian whose Euler–Lagrange equations are satisfied by every solution of the original multisymplectic system, while the Euler–Lagrange system may admit additional solutions. Remove equivalent-solution-set language from the passage.
issues.why_classification: The old calculation establishes solution-set inclusion but not the converse. Correcting the claim is contained and requires no new proof architecture, while the associated-Lagrangian construction and all recorded downstream guarantees survive. Nevertheless, withdrawing equality of solution sets is a substantive but limited weakening, so the issue exceeds minor severity without causing major mathematical loss.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: every solution of the system satisfies the Euler--Lagrange equations arising from the associated Lagrangian form $\msL$. However, just as in the continuous case, the Euler--Lagrange equations may have other solutions.

issues.title: Missing real-logarithm domain in Example 5.3

failure_location.quote: Consider the following discrete Lagrangian defined on $\mathbb{Z}^2\times P(\mathbb{R}^3)$:

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the discrete Lagrangian is defined on all of \(\mathbb Z^2\times P(\mathbb R^3)\). The displayed Hamiltonian contains the real expression \(\ln u^2_{0,0}\), which is defined only for \(u^2_{0,0}>0\), and its Euler–Lagrange equation also contains \(C/u^2_{0,0}\), which is undefined at zero. Thus the formula supports only the positive-second-component subdomain, not the declared full real fibre.
issues.overall_effect: The example and its subsequent calculations are well-defined only on the positive-second-component region. No later formal result depends on the example.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the declared fibre by `U = R × (0,∞) × R` and state that the example is defined on `Z² × P(U)`, so every relevant second component is positive. The Hamiltonian, Euler–Lagrange equations, and subsequent calculations can then remain unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The real logarithm forces positivity of its argument, and the reciprocal term confirms that zero is inadmissible. Imposing the natural domain is a short, routine local qualification that changes no calculation, conclusion, or dependent result. The defect is genuine but entails no meaningful mathematical loss.
